utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Could I ask you, please, to read the affirmation on the card in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And good morning to everyone, both Your Honours and the Defence team and also to the witness. Examined by Ms. Tuma:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can the witness please state your name.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Mara Bucko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask you what year you were born?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like you to describe your professional background. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I completed my elementary school in Djakovo. Then secondary medical school in Osijek. I started working in 1962 in Vukovar as a nurse. I continued working there until the 20th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you were working in Vukovar, were you as well living in the Vukovar -- the city of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe us just briefly about your family, if you were married at the time and had children, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I am married. I have two children, a son and a daughter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And were they as well living with you in Vukovar, let us say, in the summer 1991 and during the autumn 1991? Your children and your husband.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: My daughter, my husband, and I were living together. My son had gotten married, and once he did that, he found an apartment for himself and lived there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your husband, was he living with you?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where in Vukovar exactly were you living? Where did you have your home in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: My house was located in Sajmiste. It was located on a street called Slavonski Brigada 28.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said here that you were working as a nurse at the Vukovar Hospital. Did you have any kind of specialty? And in that case, what kind of specialty?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. Initially I worked at the surgical ward. I worked there for years. Later on, when the new building was built, I was transferred to the surgical clinic and to the emergency ward. And following that, I went to the central sterilisation department. This department prepares equipment and other supplies, sterile equipment for the wounded, for the surgeries, and other supplies needed for dressing wounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember from about what time you were working with this sterilisation or material in your career as a nurse at the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I can't remember the year, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you working in this capacity during the summer 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. I also assisted whenever needed elsewhere, with the wounded, patients, whenever there was a need.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were working in this capacity during the sterilisation of material, were there any specific parts of the hospital that you were attached to in order to perform your duties as a nurse?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. It is located at the bottom of the corridor. It's a corridor leading to the atomic shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what part of the hospital was this? We all know that there are different parts in the hospital, comprised of different buildings, so to say.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: In the new part of the hospital, in the new building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout the summer and autumn 1991, were you able to continually working at the same spot the whole time?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why then not?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Because there was bombing, destruction, and we couldn't continue working with our regular equipment. We were forced to move sterilising machines to a small room in the atomic shelter. Initially we were also able to use a part of the laboratory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This bombardment of the hospital, can you just briefly, because we heard this before from other witnesses, but can you just briefly inform us when it started and what kind of intensity it was? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: At first I was at home. It was around noon time. It was a Sunday, the 25th of August. I saw the planes flying above. I was cooking lunch but did not complete it because I was informed on the phone that once the bombing subsided, they would send a car to come and fetch me and go to work because I would need to be there if they needed extra sterilised supplies and also if they needed any extra help with the wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then go to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened afterwards? You were describing the 25th of August, that air planes were over the Vukovar city. What was afterwards the 25th of August? How was it then when it comes to the bombardment and just briefly about -- concerning the hospital itself.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: On that day, we did what we could. We helped. We took the patients from the surgical ward, which was at the second floor of the new building, downstairs. We pushed the beds into the corridor. When the bombing and shelling stopped, we would take them back to their rooms. It took -- I couldn't tell you exactly how long it took, how many days, weeks. We did it whenever needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you need to do this exercise another time?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how often was that?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say how many times we had to do that. Sometimes during a day we would have to do it more than twice. We would take them in their beds to the shelter and then back in an elevator to their rooms, but how long this lasted, I wouldn't be able to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any point in time that you needed to have the patients -- they were not able to be removed back to their rooms or the corridors?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I can't specify the time, whether this was in late September or early October. As the shelling progressed, so did the destruction. There was more and more damage to the walls, and the windows, and we kept going lower and lower. One by one floor lower. Now, when exactly this happened, I really wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it during a specific period of time that the shelling was more intensive than at other times in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. On the 5th of October, a bomb shell -- a bomb -- a plane bomb landed on a hospital in the vicinity where I was. Fortunately this bomb did not explode and this is why I'm sitting here in front of you. Throughout that month, October, and until the very end, the shelling was very intense. Our patients were in corridors and in the shelter. The entire corridor of the gynaecology ward, the corridor connecting our surgical clinic with other parts, also the corridor leading to the old building and connecting it to the new building, all the way down to the atomic shelter, it was all full.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you able -- were you at this time still staying at your private home, during the nights after your working hours?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Initially, in August, when the bombing started on the 25th of August, I went to work every day. I would spend one day at work and then one day at home. This continued until perhaps late September, mid-September or late September. Until that time, I went home when I wasn't working. After that time, I was at the hospital continuously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why then? Why couldn't you stay in your private home?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: My husband was at home in our neighbourhood. Once he came to the hospital and told me that the building -- the houses had been shelled, that our house had been damaged and torched, so this is when I decided not to go back home but rather remain at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were your services needed as well continuously at the hospital at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you went back -- you stayed at the hospital from mid-September or late September continuously until the 20th November 1991; is that correct understood from me?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your husband, where was he at that time? You left your home and -- for the hospital, and your husband and your rest of the family, where were they then?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Before he came to see me at the hospital to tell me about the houses, my husband was in our neighbourhood, in our house. When he came to see me at the hospital he remained there. Prior to that, my daughter-in-law was pregnant, and she went to an island called Krk to deliver there. She delivered a baby on the 18th of August in Rijeka. My son went - I'm not sure when - in the late August, to see his wife and he didn't come back to Vukovar. I sent my daughter to Miklosevci to a village where my husband was born. Once we were reunited, she told me that they had transferred her from that village to Ilok, and that in early October, the army took them from Ilok elsewhere. She went to Djakovo to stay with my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And how about your husband? You said that he stayed in the neighbourhood of your house. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: He remained in the house. I wouldn't be able to describe to you what he did because I was at work for 24 hours and then at home for 24 hours. What my husband did in the meantime I wouldn't be able to describe you in any detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your husband a member of any kind of unit, military unit?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: At the time, when they started organising groups in neighbourhoods, our neighbourhood was called Sajmiste, and then there was also the neighbourhood called Mitnica. They started organising defence groups and he joined one of such groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know the name of that group?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I learned that in Zagreb, once we came to Zagreb, I learned that it was called the National Guards Corps. Later on, they formed the 204th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when this was, when it was formed to the 204th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I can tell you that now, because I have seen it and heard on television. Allegedly it was established in September but I wouldn't be able to confirm that with certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet your husband -- you left for the hospital and he stayed in the house. Did you meet your husband at any time? Did he come to visit you at the hospital, for instance, and did he then -- in what way was he dressed then?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: As I've told you, I worked for 24 hours and then was at home for 24 hours. My husband used to take me to work in the car in the morning and then pick me up the following morning to take me home. And then we would be at home. Whenever he came to the hospital, he wore civilian clothes, and whenever we were at home together he was also in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him at any time wear a uniform?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see him at any time wearing -- having a weapon?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: When they got organised, street by street, they had duty shifts during which time they had a weapon that they would turn over to the next person. What kind of a weapon, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you about his actions or non-actions or behaviour so to stay? Did he have any contact in telling you what was going on, so to say?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: He said they were guarding houses, to ensure that they were not looted, so that people wouldn't go to houses that were empty and steal from them. This is what he told me. There were cases in our neighbourhoods and streets of people leaving Vukovar and leaving houses empty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us when the city of Vukovar fell?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: All I can tell you is that I heard on the 18th of August [as interpreted] that there was an agreement reached between Dr. Bosanac and Mr. Hebrang on organising an evacuation of the wounded and staff, to send them to Zagreb, to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I hear you right here, Mrs. Bucko, that you mentioned the 18th August? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No, no, no. On the 18th of November. I apologise if I made a mistake. No, no. On the 18th of November. In the afternoon hours, towards the evening, a colleague of mine told me that she had heard there would be an evacuation. This is when I learned about it. As for the fall of Vukovar, I learned about it in the morning when my husband arrived in the hospital. Then he told me that Vukovar had fallen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 18th November, were you at that time working in the hospital on that day?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us here in the courtroom what happened during that day in the hospital, just briefly? You were doing your tasking?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. Whatever was needed, to help with the wounded, bandaging, whenever any help was needed, we assisted each other always.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said here that you learned about an evacuation. Can you explain more in detail who told you that and what was the content of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I was in the corridor where the sterilising equipment was. A colleague of mine came by, I think her name was Mrgan or Mrdan, something like that. She told me that she had heard some talk that there would be an evacuation. This is what she conveyed to all of us who were down there in the basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who would be evacuated according to what you heard from your colleague?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Patients, wounded and staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at this time get any -- on that day, on the 18th of November, get any knowledge about who would organise the evacuation? Was there any talk about that or were you informed about that?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Later on, I heard that it was to be our staff members, our workers, who would be carrying the wounded, also the husbands of our personnel was also supposed to help in that process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any mention of other operators, so to say, to facilitate the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. During that day, on the 18th November, you were working in the hospital and taking care of the patients. Did you see any people arriving to the hospital on that day?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What happened? Was there anything specific during that day, additional to what you have told us, that you remember now?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I can remember anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll move on to the next day, and that is on the 19th. Were you sleeping in the hospital during the night from the 18th to the 19th?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you then tell us what happened in the morning of the 19th? You wake up and -- you woke up and can you please tell us what happened on the morning of the 19th?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: We continued caring for the patients, doing our work, whatever was needed. In the meantime, I'm not sure where exactly in the building, I met a husband of a colleague of mine, who told me, "Your husband had arrived. He is up there in the corridor of the internal diseases ward." I went upstairs to find him. In the hall, there were many people. I found him. I took him downstairs. I went to see nurse Binazija Kolesar, and I told her that, if possible, my husband could also carry the wounded, as had been discussed previously, that husbands would be assisting with carrying the wounded. She agreed. She gave him a coat. He took his coat off and he left it in the room where we were, and he put on the coat that she had given him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of coat was that?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: You mean the white one? Or you mean his coat?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The coat he was given by Kolesar to put on.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: It was short, it was white, it was a coat-type coat. It wasn't a long one but, rather, a short one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why couldn't he use his civilian clothing when helping out with the wounded patients?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Because it was very dirty, and he was too, but then he changed and he had a wash, in order to be cleaner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you met him here in the morning, what -- for what purpose did he come to see you in the hospital? What did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: He was at the Eltz castle. Because when he came to see me at the hospital, he stayed there for a while. He helped with different types of work, closing windows so that it's not too cold. Perhaps that was the end of September, beginning of October. I don't know exactly. One evening, some people came, some people I don't know. They got a few of them and took them away. They said that they had to be at their positions, and the position he got was the Eltz castle. And he was there until the fall. On the morning of the 19th, and that's what he told me later, their commander came and said, "What are you still doing there? The army is at the bridge. It would be best for you to go to the hospital." And my husband set out and that's how he reached me at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he want to do in the hospital? What did he tell you in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: He told me that Sremac told him that Vukovar had fallen and then I told you we went to see nurse Biba. He intended to help with carrying the wounded patients when they were evacuated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have the capacity to help out with the patients while he did not have any kind of training to do that, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say, but one is capable of carrying stretchers and pushing gurneys, and we would transfer patients from beds to stretchers. And if beds were supposed to be pushed with patients on them, then again you could help there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So he received the white coat and he put it on. And this was in the morning on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- during that day?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Well, you see, I was with my colleagues, and he was walking around the hospital, the corridors of the hospital. People were talking, feeling this uncertainty. We were all looking at each other. Some with greater fear, some with lesser fear. I cannot really tell you that I was thinking of anything in particular.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened during that day? Were there any evacuation?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you experience during -- otherwise during that day in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Well, things were normal, like until then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any soldiers in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Well, it was around noon or perhaps a bit after midday. I wasn't looking at my watch, and I cannot tell you exactly but that's when the army arrived, and I saw Arivani [phoen] at the entrance into the emergency ward. Didn't see him in the building, though. A man who I knew, he was sitting on a stretcher at the entrance into the hospital, and two or three other persons, I cannot give you an exact number. He wore civilian trousers, a green jacket, and he had a fur hat on his head, Maksimovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said here that the army arrived at the hospital. What army arrived? Can you --

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. The Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. I saw young boys, young men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you recognise it was the JNA, the people's Yugoslav army that arrived at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: They wore olive green uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say approximately how many you saw arriving, the JNA soldiers, arriving to the hospital on that day, the 19th November?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I cannot give you any numbers. I saw a few of them, and I didn't see them a lot during the course of the day. In the afternoon, when we were asked to come to the plaster room, the staff were asked to come there, Mr. Veselin Sljivancanin made a speech to us and said that on that day, there could be no evacuation, that it was already late, that it would take place on the following day. He said that we could go on working in hospital because staff would be needed. He also told me, since I worked on the equipment for central sterilisation to stay there, and Biba Kolesar, nurse Biba Kolesar, the head nurse, should stay and that a few of us should stay working at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this happened? When did you meet the Major Sljivancanin at the hospital? It was on the 19th but can you remember what -- during what day -- what part of the day you saw him, or you met him?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I think that was in the afternoon, early evening. I cannot give you the exact time. I wasn't really paying any attention to the time. I didn't even know what day it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you meet him? Can you describe us more in detail what happened? Were you told to see him or to see someone else? Can you more in detail describe for us this event?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: We came to the plaster room. The staff were told to come to the plaster room. That's when Mr. Sljivancanin made a speech to us. He came to the plaster room. Now, had he already been at the plaster room or did he arrive subsequently, I really don't know. I can't remember. And he made that speech to us, as I already told you. And also, he said that Dr. Bosanac was no longer director of the hospital, that a major would take her place. I can't remember the name of the major, that he would be in charge of the hospital now, and then he told us that we should stay there and go on working.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that it was Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: In the plaster room, he introduced himself. Now, did he say that he was a major or did he hold some other rank, I cannot say, but he did say that he was Veselin Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that speech, did he say anything about the medical staff?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. If we want to, that we can stay and go on working. Nothing else. And he said that on that day there could be no evacuation, that it would take place on the following day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he mention any other categories of people in that sense?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how about the family members of the medical staff?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That our families could come with us when the evacuation takes place. That our husbands could accompany us, the staff members, once we were evacuated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you could watch leading, Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I know, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anything else happened during that meeting that you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were there? You mentioned that "we" were in that room. Who were "we"?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Nurses of the medical centre, of the general hospital in Vukovar. Not all of them but a few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many about?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Well, I cannot give you an exact number but perhaps 40, 30, I don't know, 50.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you between the night between the 19th and the following day, the 20th November?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: In a small room near the central sterilisation. A few of my colleagues were there and my husband was there and we were sitting and talking, awaiting the next day, to see what would happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened next day in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: In the morning, somebody knocked at the door, that the nurses were supposed to go to the plaster room for a talk. We told my husband to stay there and he said that he didn't want to. He went out so I locked the little room and I went to the plaster room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that somebody knocked at the door. Did you see that person?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see that person?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe that person, please?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: A youngish man in uniform. He just told us to go to the plaster room, and then we slowly got ready and went there. He went further on down the corridor towards the central shelter, to call others as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say for what reason he knocked on the door?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you -- what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: He told us to come to the plaster room for a talk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say who would talk to you?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do after that man, that person, talked to you?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: From that corridor, we slowly went down to the plaster room, those of us who were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who are "we"?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Well, nurses. The nurses who were there with me on that night in that little room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: To the plaster room, down the corridor. We took the route that leads to the plaster room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were in the plaster room?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Our staff was already there, and then Mr. Veselin Sljivancanin came. He started talking to us, telling us that that gentleman, the major, who was to be the director of the hospital, or rather, he introduced him and he was also there and talked about the work of the hospital, saying that we should stay on, work there, that if a few of us stayed there, we could stay with our family, relatives, get a few days of rest, and then return to work at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there -- did they say anything about the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they say anything -- well, who were addressing you? Was it more than one person or was this only one person addressing you in that plaster room?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: In the plaster room, it was Mr. Sljivancanin who spoke to us. And now was it in the afternoon of the 19th or the morning of the 20th, when this new director of the hospital spoke to us, that is something I cannot tell you with any degree of certainty, what the day was, what the date was. But at any rate, both of them addressed us and said that he was now the new director, that Mrs. Bosanac, Dr. Bosanac, was no longer the director, that we now had to follow his orders, and that they would be in charge, issuing orders from now on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were in that plaster room?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Well, I think 30, 40, 50, something like that. The rest were in the corridor leading from the plaster room to the other waiting room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Sljivancanin addressed you, in what way did he address you at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Well, he was a tall man, a proud man. How should I put this? Stable. He spoke clearly, he was issuing orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To whom did he issue orders and what kind of orders was issued?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Well, he was telling us that we had to listen to them now, that the new director of the hospital was there, and that we should stay there, go on working, that nothing would happen to us, that we should feel free to stay at the hospital and work there. That was what was said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How long were you -- how long did this meeting take, about? I do understand it's difficult ten years after, but can you have any kind of feeling how long time this meeting took?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I really cannot say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you observe anything when you were in the plaster room?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: While we were in the plaster room, Mrs. Selebaj came, a nurse, and she said, "Your husband is looking for you." She said that to me. For a moment I went out to the door. He said to me, "You are there shut up in the plaster room, while they are taking us away. I will have to leave too. Give me the key so that I can take my jacket." And then he took off that jacket from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he exactly say; do you remember that? And how did he look like when he said it?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: He was frightened. I'm not sure but I think that this is what he said: "We are being taken away while you were shut up into the plaster room. And I will have to go, to go," most probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he mean by "we"? Do you know that? Did he say that to you?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No. We didn't talk for very long either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next? Did you stay in the room with your husband, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No. I went back to the plaster room. It was probably already the end of the talk by then, and then Mr. Sljivancanin asked if there was anybody who had any questions. And I said, "I do." I raised my hand and I said, "I do. You promised us yesterday that our husbands could come with us. And now you took them away." Mr. Sljivancanin answered that that was not true, that they were there. Then I replied that what he said was not true. They were taken away. But where, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you okay, Mrs. Bucko? We can take a pause here. I do understand it's difficult for you. But it's okay and we can take a pause now, if Their Honours -- or can you handle this?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: It's all right, it's all right. I can handle it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Since I handled all of that, I guess I can handle this too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just take your time and take it easy. It's fine.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Then I said to this gentleman that they had taken away our husbands. He said to me, then, "Take a piece of paper and a pencil. Write down your husbands' names and we will bring them there. But only if they have no blood on their hands." I went to another room, which is the surgery, I took a piece of paper from a drawer, I had a pen in my pocket, and I started writing down names. I wanted to give this same piece of paper to other people in the hallway so that there would be as many names as possible on this piece of paper. Mr. Sljivancanin wouldn't let me do that. So then this piece of paper was returned to the plaster room, and we had to hand it over to him. When we gave him this piece of paper, there were 15, 16, 17 names on that list. I cannot give you an exact number. He took this piece of paper and said that he would send someone to pick them up. I don't know who Mr. Sljivancanin sent. Nor did I see. We left the plaster room. I saw that my husband was not there. After that, I ran around the hospital compound looking for them. However, I saw many people on the right-hand side of the emergency entrance and on the left-hand side too. And they said that these masses of people standing on the right side were going to Novi Sad, and on the left side, they would be going to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Bucko. You said that you took a piece of paper and you had the pen in your pocket and you put names on that piece of paper, and you also said it was about 15 to 16 names. Who were they? What kind of names and people did you put on that list?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Kolesar, Stanek, Sic, Selebaj, both he and his father, that is. Then this man who our Rada lived with. I don't know his name. Rada, she's a nurse, and she lived with this man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those names that you have mentioned now, who were they? Were they attached to anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Husbands. Husbands of our staff members. I haven't mentioned my husband yet. I wanted to mention his name last. I thought I'd remember some other names before that but I really cannot recall all the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Bucko. You said also here that you handed that piece of paper over to Sljivancanin. Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Well, he asked us. He wanted us to give him back the paper with the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you try not to?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you want to do with that list?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: It actually went through my mind that if he sent them back, perhaps we would be able to save them. We didn't know what was going to happen to us but I thought if he was with me, he and I would share the same fate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Bucko, when you're saying that, you thought that you can save them, what do you mean by "save"?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Since he promised us that nothing would happen to us, to the medical staff, and to our husbands, I believed that we would be saved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Saved from what?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you precisely, saved from what. He just said that -- I thought we would be saved. I don't know from what. I didn't know where they were going, where people were being taken, or why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you afraid?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Very much so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for what?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Listen, I was afraid of everything. I didn't know where we would be going, how. Our house was destroyed. I didn't know what would happen to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Bucko. You said that you left the plaster room.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you okay, Mrs. Bucko? Okay. You said you left the plaster room. Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I went outside to look for my husband because I didn't see him in the corridor, which is where we spoke the last time, in the corridor right next to the plaster room. I went around the compound looking for him. I didn't find him. I begged, I ran around looking for him, and then nurse Biba joined me also looking for her husband as did our other colleagues. They all went whenever they could all over the compound looking. Then I turned to Dr. Ivankovic, asking him to help us with the new director of the hospital, to see if he was able to help us to ensure that our husbands would come with us. Dr. Ivankovic went to a small room, which was our small surgery that we used to treat patients who needed suturing. Dr. Ivankovic explained what our request was. The new director got up and said he would help us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened next? You were on that surgery room --

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: As I was running around the compound, on the opposite entrance, on the other side of the compound, across from the hospital, I saw a bus. I ran up to that bus. I wanted to talk to my husband, whom I saw there. A soldier, youngish one, in a uniform, I assume it was a military uniform, prevented me from doing that. I came up to the window, towards the end of the bus. I knocked on the window but was unable to establish communication. Once again, I ran back to the hospital. Nurse Biba was with me, Dr. Ivankovic and the new director. We talked, and then we came outside. We saw Mr. Sljivancanin standing outside with our Bogdan. Our husbands had already been taken off the bus, lined up next to the sidewalk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened next? They were lined -- your husbands were lined up by the sidewalk. And where were you then when you saw that?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: At the back gate, on the left side, this is where they were lined up, we went outside to ask Mr. Sljivancanin to let them go. The new director said that the names of my husband and Biba's husband should be called out. He called out their names. We were slowly approaching him. He asked Bogdan -- I think that Mr. Sljivancanin asked Bogdan whether Bogdan knew my husband. He said no. Then my husband supposedly was asked whether he knew Bogdan, and my husband said no. Mr. Sljivancanin said, "Go. Get lost." And I thought at that moment, you can tell us to get lost all you want. Just let us live on, get on with our lives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Bucko. You said that you asked Sljivancanin, or you and the others, asked Sljivancanin to let them go. Why did you approach Sljivancanin to ask that?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Well, because I had contact with him in the plaster room, because I gave him the list with the names. That's why I thought that he was in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he reply?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I don't understand what you are saying. When?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Sljivancanin was asked to let them go, what did he -- did he say anything then? Or did he do anything?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No. He just asked Bogdan this, and then said to my husband, "Get lost." Afterwards I didn't hear anything else. Other people remained there. My husband and I left that place, went to another side of the compound, and stood there. On the other side, there were buses waiting to take us elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your description here, you said that you were running around the compound and you saw a bus. Where were that bus located?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I don't know what bus you have in mind. The one that had brought them in in Gunduliceva Street?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned here during the description that you saw a bus when you were running around the compound, that bus that you later on approached. Where was that bus located?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: That street was in Gunduliceva Street. When I went out, I saw him in Gunduliceva Street, the bus. I approached the bus, I saw there were people there. I came to the door and the gentleman, the youngish one in a uniform, didn't let me go in. Then I went all the way back to the back of the bus. I knocked on the window and was unable to establish communication with my husband.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see your husband in the bus?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other people in the bus at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Kolja Selebaj. Sic. I can't remember now the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Then you said that the husbands were outside on the pavement. Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. They were lined up, one next to each other. They stood in one line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers around?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said earlier on there was a young man on the bus and he was not able to establish contact. What kind of man was that?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: The soldier stood at the door of the bus, and the men were inside the bus. I wanted to get on the bus or have my husband come out of the bus, but we weren't able to do either of the two. This is why I went and knocked on the window, trying to get my husband's attention, to tell him, I don't know what I was going to tell him, but something to the effect that he should get off the bus. I just wanted us to stay together and then go elsewhere together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That soldier that you just mentioned, what kind of soldier was it? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: A youngish man, but I wouldn't be able to describe to you his appearance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what kind of army he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. He had an olive-green uniform. Whether this was a JNA uniform I wouldn't be able to tell you with certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next? Did you meet your husband?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: We went back towards the main gate, which is where the buses were lined up. Dr. Ivankovic wished us a safe trip. We stood there, and then as we were approaching that place, we boarded the buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who are "we"?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: My husband and I.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other people boarded the buses? What kind of -- what categories were they?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. People from the hospital, who happened to be at the hospital on that day. They got on to several buses. I wouldn't be able to tell you exactly how many buses there were. We boarded the buses and sat there waiting for them to depart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said it was people from the hospital. Can you more describe what that contained of, people from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: The staff who worked there, cleaning ladies and nurses, medical technicians, all of us who were in the hospital got on the buses, except for those who remained there. The rest of us got on the buses. But before my husband and I got there, there were already people inside the buses, but I wouldn't be able to tell you how many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Patients, where were they?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know that. I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened next? You boarded the bus together with your husband?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: We went through the centre of the town, through Radiceva Street, Senoa Street, Sajmiste. We passed the area where my house is. We travelled in the direction of Velepromet, turned right on to Petrovacka road. At the end of that area, there is a building of the textile industry facility. There were a lot of women inside. They waved to us and knocked on the windows. We remained sitting in the bus. We stopped there for a while. They didn't take us through Petrovac to Croatia but rather the buses turned back, via Negoslavci, Oriolik, Tovarnik, Sid, and went to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened there?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: In Sremska Mitrovica, once we arrived there, we heard that this facility was some kind of an athletic centre. It was dark, so I didn't see the building clearly. I wouldn't be able to describe it to you. We couldn't get inside the building because there had already been a lot of people there. We got off the bus, thinking that we would get inside the building. There was no room for us there so we went back on the bus and then they drove us to another holding centre. I don't know what it was called. I wasn't interested in learning either. There, we spent the entire night in the bus, in that compound. The following day, in the morning, we were taken further on. I think we came to Bosnia, and there they exchanged us. People got from one bus on to another bus, and we were then taken to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Bucko. I will now -- you gave us the whole -- your whole story here, what you saw and experienced in the hospital during those days and before that. I would like to ask you, because you did approach Mr. Sljivancanin a couple of times, as we have heard here, in the hospital, what kind of approach did he gave you? What kind of manner, what kind of approach did he gave you? What did you see him as? Please describe that for us.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: My impression, a tall man, a well-built one, with a moustache. How should I describe it to you? He had an articulate way of speaking. He was proud. And my personal impression was that he was very important and that was his own attitude about it. He was in charge there. He was the commander. And we had to listen to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Bucko. You said that he was a commander. Can you describe that in more detail why you had that impression?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: In the plaster room, I talked to him twice. Afterwards, I didn't, based on his attitude.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of attitude was that?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: As I've already described it to you, he was somebody who spoke sternly. I don't know how else to describe it to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Bucko.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a correction for the transcript, page 28, line 21 and 22. When asked by my learned friend about the events in Bosnia, I think that the witness said that they changed the buses, went from one bus to another, whereas in the transcript, it appears as though they were exchanged. I think that they just changed the buses but were not exchanged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps you could check on that, Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Bucko, did you hear the comment from Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please clarify that for us.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The buses stopped. We got off the bus. We came outside. We left the buses in which we had arrived, and then a little bit further away, there stood other buses that we boarded. In our bus, here before this Trial Chamber, I want to express the gratitude to the driver who drove us. He was very kind and he apologised to us, telling us that he didn't do this of his own free will. This is what he told us as he drove us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you supposed to be exchanged or were there change between buses? Did you change from one bus to another, if I understood Mr. Vasic right?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. We got off one set of buses and went into another set of buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mrs. Bucko.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm done with the examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mrs. Tuma. That's obviously a convenient time now for a break. We will resume sitting at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet. Cross-examined by Mr. Domazet:

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. Good morning, Mrs. Bucko.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me introduce myself. I'm Vladomir Domazet, Defence counsel for Mr. Mrksic, and I'm going to put a few questions to you. Today when answering the questions of my learned friend, you said that the first bombing of Vukovar took place exactly on Sunday, the 25th of October -- August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: The 25th of August, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, did you personally see or hear, or did you perhaps hear later, that a day before these events about which you testified, an aircraft of the JNA air force was downed near Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "no" are you saying that you've never heard of any such thing or only at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: At that time, I did not hear that a plane had been downed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about later?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: In conversations while we were in hospital, at work, people talked about this downing and this was already the beginning of November. I cannot tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You cannot say when it was downed. I understand that fully. Thank you. On that day, the 25th of August, the day that you're talking about as the day of the first bombing, was the hospital hit or was it hit somewhat later in the way that you described?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly about that day, whether it was hit, but on that afternoon, we were taking our patients down to the basement, to the corridors that were lower down. I was home and I was asked to come in to work. On a corner in Vukovar, I saw a car that had burned down, and they told me that it was due to the bombing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Today you said that because of such situations, for a while you were compelled to take your patients down to the ground floor or to the shelter and then to return them by elevator, that this situation prevailed for a while. If I understood you correctly, you cannot say exactly how long this lasted, but it was until the end of September, beginning of October. Is that what you said today?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I think it could have been that way until September. I don't know exactly. I cannot give you an exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But for a while, that's the way it was?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: For a while, that's the way it was. That is how patients were taken care of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Bucko, while you were still at home and while you went to work, you said that your husband would take you by car in the morning and that he would meet you the next morning, and it was my understanding that you worked the way people employed in the health service usually did work. For 24 hours. Did I understand you correctly that you had a 24-hour shift and then you had a break that was as long or a bit shorter?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: As long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So this is the period while you were at home. When you started spending nights at the hospital, to when you were in hospital all the time, did you have the same kind of breaks or did you already start working in different ways?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Sometimes it would be that same kind of break and sometimes, when necessary, we worked again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you talked about this period, that is to say the time when you stayed in the hospital at night as well, you said that that was after your husband said that your house was damaged and that's when you decided to stay on in the hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, was your husband already mobilised for the military or did he volunteer? I don't know how he joined the ZNG. You already mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I said that in different neighbourhoods that is how they were organised, and that's when he joined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understood you correctly, he and others, for the most part from the neighbourhood, were on guard duty with weapons and then they would return the weapons at the end of their guard shift; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, you mentioned in your answers today to my learned friend that for a while your husband was at the Eltz castle. I think that's the name of the castle.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that after this first task that we had -- that he had, that he was reassigned to Eltz later?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. When he came to stay with me at the hospital, they came and they took a few civilians away from the hospital, and he said that he was at the Eltz castle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. So that's what you know from what he told you?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: What he told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never went there yourself at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you tell me now that he came and took away a few civilians, what was this all about? Were they patients, some wounded persons, that he took from hospital? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Well, either two or three men came. They picked up a few of our husbands and they took them away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Took them away? You mean there, to the positions at this castle?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes, there. When this man came, I don't know what his name is, I don't know who he is, I don't know what position he held, I asked him where he was, just like I asked Mr. Sljivancanin about my husband. Then I also spoke to this man about my husband and he told me that they were taken to these positions at this hospital -- at this castle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall perhaps from that moment onwards, when your husband was somewhere at the Eltz castle, these positions there, until November when he came to the hospital, that is to say the 19th of November, did you see him in the meantime or not?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did this happen? Did he come? Because you said you didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: He came to the hospital to see me, and then he would return.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that you had no other way of communicating. Or perhaps you did. Could you communicate by telephone or something?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that around the 18th of November, sometime in the afternoon, you heard from your colleague that an evacuation was being prepared. If I understand you correctly, you could not inform your husband about that in any way?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, you did say that on the following morning, the morning of the 19th, he came and he himself told you that Vukovar had fallen and that his commander said that he should come to the hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you that he came on his own or with some other colleagues of his?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Stanek came, Vasos [phoen], I think, and I don't know whether there was yet another man there or not. I cannot tell you for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I see that you know the names or surnames of these people. You can identify them. You probably know them. Who were they?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Stanek was the husband of one of our nurses, Marica Stanek. As for Vasos, my husband knew him, and I had met him earlier too. I don't know him in any other way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he had nothing to do with the hospital. I mean, his wife was not employed at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I don't know about Vasos. As for Stanek, his wife worked at the hospital, just like I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said something else after saying that on that same morning their commander said what he said to him. And then you said, Sremac said to them. Is Sremac a surname or is that perhaps the surname of this commander?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Stanko Sremac or Stanislav Sremac, I don't know exactly. That's the name and surname of their commander. That is what my husband told me. And I made my conclusions on the basis of that, because he said that that was their commander. I never saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you heard about the preparation of the evacuation for the first time on the afternoon of the 18th or in the early evening from your colleague, Mrgan, or that was a name that you mentioned, I think.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she mention any details to you or was this sort of in general terms, that it was announced that there would be some kind of evacuation?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: That it was just announced that there would be an evacuation. No other details. She did not tell me about any other details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A bit later, you said that you had asked nurse Kolesar, who was the head nurse at surgery?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That you asked her if your husband could stay and help during the planned evacuation so that in a way he could assist with the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. When he came back from the castle, that morning, but that is the 19th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. That was after he came, because you yourself said that you didn't know that he would come and he did not know about this either. So I'm talking about the 19th, after he came back.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that his wish, or did you yourself think of that and do it?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Well, that is what both of us agreed upon, and we thought, well, we should go together and whatever happens to us happens to us while we are together. Our children were already not with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether your colleague did the same thing, the lady whose husband came together with your husband?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I don't know about that because we didn't talk about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry but I'd like to go back to the previous day, the 18th. My learned friend asked you whether you noticed some people coming to the hospital then. I think that you answered that you could not remember. I would like to try to ask you whether you specifically saw many more people coming to the hospital than was customary, primarily civilians, men and women, more civilians than usual coming in on that afternoon. Did you perhaps notice that?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: On the 18th, I did not see that. But on the 19th, when I went up to the hall to pick up my husband, there were many civilians in the hall. I don't know when they came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you can confirm that for the 19th. As for the 18th, you stand by what you said, that you cannot remember specifically any people coming?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who Marin Vidic, nicknamed Bili, was?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I heard the name but I didn't know him. I heard that he was either the president of our municipality or whatever. I cannot tell you exactly. I heard of him, but I didn't know him personally, nor did I see him before I came to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you told me that you had not seen him yourself until you came to Zagreb, did you hear from someone that on the 18th and the 19th and 20th of November, Mr. Vidic was in hospital?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I did not see him. Perhaps he passed by. I did not know the man, so I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So at that time, you didn't know what he looked like physically, if I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you talked about the 19th, and when you were informed by your colleague that your husband was in the hall, you said that you saw many people there and that in a way you had trouble finding him because there were so many people there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, first and foremost, when you're talking about the hall, let's check this. You're probably talking about the ground floor of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: That's right. The ground floor of the hospital by the entrance into the hospital, and from there, you went upstairs or, rather, you took elevators upstairs while the hospital worked normally. But the hall is the ground floor or, rather, on the first floor. And as for the ground floor, it was even lower. It was where we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few moments ago, you told me, once again, that there were many people there. Did you have time to notice who these people were or were you focused on finding your husband? Did you recognise anyone? Could you tell us who these people were who were in the hall?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I cannot say who these people were because I was looking for my husband. I did not pay attention to other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's quite logical. Now I would like to ask you something about these white coats that were mentioned. What was the usual dressing code for you who worked at the hospital? What about the doctors? Did the doctors wear white coats or some other kind of coats? What did they wear?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: There were white coats and there were also green ones for the operating room. However, people wore them also in corridors. I don't know whether there was a sufficient number of them. People also had green trousers and coats. There were that types of uniforms as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is what you're saying to us, those who were worked in operating rooms, they wore green uniforms, green trousers and shirts or coats, tops?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the nurses? How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I had a uniform. I had a skirt and a blouse. It was white and blue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did people wear blue uniforms and white uniforms? Was there -- how were they distinguished?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No. There was nothing to distinguish the time for wearing one or the other. We wore them whenever necessary. We wore what we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell us, please, did the doctors and other staff wear also short coats or jackets, white jackets, which were short? Is that what the doctors wore?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: We had them at the hospital, but I wouldn't be able to tell you now who wear precisely what kind of a uniform, and when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. People had longer coats and shorter coats. Yes. There were different kinds of tops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You told us about the doctors, nurses, and then you also had auxiliary personnel who were not medical staff but were there to assist you. What about them? What did they wear?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: They wore grey and pink uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is how one could tell them apart?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: That was before this evil erupted. Afterwards, we wore what we had. We wore what we could get our hands on. Paediatric nurses wore pink clothes. Our cleaning ladies wore grey clothes, and nurses wore blue uniforms, whereas the doctors wore white ones. Later on, it was all mixed. Nurses would wear white uniforms. They would wear what they had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But I'm now referring to auxiliary personnel, cleaning people, orderlies and so on, people who were there to assist you, who were not medically trained.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I think that our workers had some kind of blue coats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Let us go back to the 19th. You went to Mrs. Kolesar to ask her if your husband could stay with you and help carry the wounded and also do some other tasks related to evacuation. She agreed, and you said she gave him a white coat. Was there something on the coat indicating that he was part of medical personnel? Do you know why she gave him that coat? Were there many such cases?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: There was nothing on that coat, no -- nothing to tell that he was part of medical personnel. We asked for him to change his clothes because his jacket was quite dirty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you understood what I was driving at. He could have been given a blue uniform because he was just there to assist. What -- what was the decisive factor in him being give and white coat?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I don't know. Nurse Biba gave him the coat and I don't know why she gave him precisely that one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Bucko, today in examination-in-chief, you said something that you also said when giving your statement. You described a man wearing a fur coat and some other type of clothing together with other men. I would like to ask you something related to that. Were these people in any way prevented from entering the hospital, and if so, by whom?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: There was a younger man there wearing a uniform. He didn't let them enter through the emergency entrance, and they were left standing outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. This is what you said in your statement, and I just wanted to confirm that. Based on what you said today, I could tell that you were able to clearly distinguish between the regular JNA soldiers at the time and others based on their appearance and their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Listen, based on what I know, the JNA soldiers wore olive-green uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that somebody was introduced to you but you couldn't remember whether it was on the 18th in the afternoon or on the 19th but there was a major who was introduced to you as the future hospital director. Did he say or perhaps did somebody else say that this man was from the military medical academy and that this hospital from now on would be under the auspices of that institution?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to confirm that. I don't remember. I think that this was mentioned, but I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Then you spoke about the 19th, the evening of the 19th. You said that your husband was with you, that all of you were together, you and some other colleagues of yours were in a room where you normally spent the night whenever at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is this room located? Can you describe that?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Right by the central sterilisation department, where we kept the supplies that had been prepared for sterilisation, gloves, coats, trousers, whatever we had to sterilise for surgeries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So there is -- there was a room next to the room where you stayed?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to these rooms, including the corridor, were there patients and the wounded staying there already?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. There was a corridor where there were already patients, and then lower, there was a slope leading to another corridor, and on the right there was a corridor leading to the atomic shelter, and the other part of the corridor led to the old hospital building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So if I understood you well, once you left the room where you spent your nights, the areas were full of patients, beds and so on?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. Our patients were all over the hospital, in the corridors, shelter, everywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you spent many nights with these persons. Who were the nurses that were there with you, that night and previously?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Perovic, Magda, who also worked in the sterilisation department, Jelka Novak, Vera Graf. I think Jelka Selebaj was there as well. My husband and I. We were there that night. I'm not fully certain about Jelka Selebaj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Jelka Selebaj, did she also have a husband who was at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Her husband was also at the hospital, as was her father-in-law, her husband's father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us clarify a name. I think there is a mistake in the transcript. Would you please repeat the name. Mrs. Novak, what's her first name?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Ilonka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ilonka, all right. I just wanted to clarify that. You told us today that on that night you stayed up quite late talking. My impression was that you either didn't sleep that night or slept very little. Am I right in concluding this? Did you stay up quite long talking with your colleagues and your husband?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: We stayed up for a long time talking in the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
