utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember whether that night there was anything else remarkable? First of all, tell us, was it peaceful at the hospital when you were there in that room?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I personally didn't see or hear anything. I was in the room. As for the other parts of the hospital, I can't tell you anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You say yourself that you didn't hear anything that night. Did you hear on the following morning whether anything had happened that previous night?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now that we are discussing this topic, let me ask you: Do you know the name of the husband of Ilonka Novak?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I believe it's Veljko Novak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said today that sometime in the morning, I'm not going to ask you about the time because I see that you had difficulties there, but at any rate you said that in the morning, a soldier knocked on your door and told you that all medical personnel should assemble in the plaster room; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that there was a certain number of people there, based on your recollection. My question is: Did you see Dr. Bosanac in the plaster room?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No, I didn't see her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Dr. Njavro?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Dr. Ivankovic?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: In the plaster room? I can't confirm that I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about him, about seeing him somewhat later but you don't remember seeing him in the plaster room. What about Dr. Njavro? Do you remember seeing him later, just like you saw Dr. Ivankovic?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described to us how your husband came. You said that you left the room and then your husband said to you, "Well, you are shut in there. They are taking us away." He also asked for the key of the room so that he could go and get his jacket. Based on what you said, it seems to me that you were not really shut in that room. You were able to leave it because you left it yourself when Mrs. Selebaj told you to come out. You were not locked in that room, were you?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No. We were not locked in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were able to come out whenever you wanted?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. I came to the door, and while standing in the door, I talked to my husband and then went back. I was able to come in and get out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that your husband asked for the key of the room so he could go and get his jacket and also -- did you say that he also returned the white coat? I didn't quite understand that part.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: He said he wanted to get his jacket. I don't know whether he took off the coat and left it or not because I didn't see later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next time you saw your husband, was he wearing his jacket or the white coat?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Jacket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He didn't have the white coat either on him or wasn't holding it in his hands?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It seemed to me that you said that he had told you he was returning the white coat but you don't remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No, no. We didn't spend a lot of time talking there. He just asked for the key. I gave him the key. And he said that he would change his clothes, take his coat. He said, "You are shut in the plaster room and they are taking us away." We didn't discuss anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You had some trouble speaking about the fear you were experiencing at the time. Can you please tell us, can you explain that fear of yours? I assume that you and your husband had no reason to fear the JNA, which at the time was the army, armed force, of Yugoslavia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I was concerned about what was going to happen to us, where we would go. I can't tell you how these sentiments originated. I simply thought the two of us are here, our children are not with us any longer. I don't know where they are, what's going on with them. It wasn't easy for me to leave my children and to go on working. But I kept thinking I'm already of a certain age, I don't know whether I will be able to find another job elsewhere. I have to continue working here throughout the war, because I have to find a living for myself. I have to earn my retirement, and these are the motives that prompted me to remain working at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. Thank you. Will you please calm down? I didn't intend for my question to cause these difficulties. I simply wanted to get an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. Our family was separated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you just one more thing. Were there any stories circulating or any propaganda, something that you heard from something else, that could cause this fear to arise?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear anything from anybody. This is something that originated in me personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you perhaps hear at the time on that day that only a day before that a big group at Mitnica, almost 200 people, had surrendered without any problems?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I heard about that later when I was in Zagreb, when we were talking about our experiences from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you talked about the bus, where you saw your husband, was this after the bus had been returned or do you think that it was there all along, that it never went anywhere, or do you think that it was returned after the intervention you talked about?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I think that it was returned after the intervention that I told you about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you refer to a certain Bogdan, is that the Bogdan who worked in your hospital before the war?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you said that you went to the buses that were waiting, when you were there with your husband and that there were some people there already, these were staff members and family members. So were other staff members taking their family members on these buses that you took when leaving the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I cannot confirm how many family members there were in there. I could recognise the staff members because they were already on the buses. With my husband, I came to one of the last buses because I was waiting for him, I was trying to save him, I wanted us to be together no matter what happened. Time was passing. People had already boarded the buses without me seeing them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And when these buses left, you told us today and in your statement you even described the streets that the bus took, and I assume that you followed this very well even the direction that you were moving in. If I understood you correctly, the direction is the usual one whether going to Croatia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: The bus returned from the hospital towards the eastern part of Croatia, and we could go to Zagreb to the west. That was the village of Nustar, nearby, perhaps only about 20 kilometres away. That's how we could get to Croatia. No, we were not driven around on the buses. We were not driven around streets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. But I thought that you said that the buses first went in that direction. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: From Velepromet, the bus turned right to the road leading to Petrovci, and at this big curve, the road is very wide, and that is where the bus made a U-turn, saying that we had to go to Serbia because Tudjman wouldn't take us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. My question was where the U-turn was made and in which way. Did the buses stop? Did somebody intervene? Did somebody say something? You said -- what you said just now, that allegedly, Croatia, Tudjman, did not want you.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: These buses stood by the textile industry factory where we saw detained women. Now, who was saying that Croatia would not have us, I cannot tell you. I cannot describe that person for you. But we were saying that to each other, and the buses went back to Negoslavci and from Negoslavci, Oriolik, from Oriolik to -- I already told you to Tovarnik, Sid, Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want the transcript to finish. So before you went in the direction that you just described, you mentioned Petrovci, in that direction. I'm asking you, was that the road to Vinkovci until then?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: How we got to Petrovci, we could have reached Vinkovci, yes. It would have been closer than going to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understood you correctly, you said that in Sremska Mitrovica you first stopped in front of a sports centre but it was packed and that you couldn't stay there.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: That's right. We left the bus, we got to the sports hall, it was full, they took us back. I can't say who it was. They just told us, "Go back to the buses," and that's what we did. And I heard that this was some kind of a holding centre. I don't know what kind. It was night-time. I didn't really pay any attention to this. We sat on the bus all night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, there wasn't enough room for you to stay there and you spent the night on the buses and then in the morning you went further on.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: The following morning, when we went further on, we went to the toilet in that building, and there were people down there but who these people were, I really don't know. There weren't that many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't recognise these people?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No. But that's where the mother of our nurse Biba died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that the transcript does not reflect one of your sentences. You said that you saw people there who were lying on stretchers?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that these buses first entered Bosnia and that that's where the buses were changed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: It is my opinion, and that's what they were saying, that we were going via Bosnia. Now, whether that is the territory of Bosnia or Serbia still or some other territory, I cannot say. We were told that it was Bosnia. That's where we got off the bus that we came on and then we entered, boarded, other buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You explained that, and you said that there was no exchange there. But nevertheless, I'm going to ask you: There weren't any other people getting off those buses and entering the buses that you had taken until then. It was my understanding that from these first buses you boarded other buses that were waiting for you and that were empty?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Empty buses. And what happened to the buses that stayed behind, whether they were taken back or wherever, that is something I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So we've completed that subject. Mrs. Bucko, I'd like to ask you something now that has to do with life at the hospital and life in Vukovar before all of these things happened. You said that you lived in an area that was called Sajmiste; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this a part of town with a population that had quite a few Serb and Croat families?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: In my neighbourhood, in my street, I can say that there were quite a few Serbs, if not half/half, then perhaps in some parts they were even a majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That's the kind of figures I saw too about that.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I can even list them all for you, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you say that you know them personally, I assume that you had some kind of relationships there. What was your relationship with your Serb neighbours until the '90s, until 1991 to be precise?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Until things started happening in Borovo Selo, we had excellent relations. We talked, we visited each other. When Borovo Selo started, then they started avoiding us and they stopped talking to us. So these contacts weakened. And they started leaving their houses, going away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was it that suddenly caused this change? Because if you are talking about the incident in Borovo Selo that I have in mind, namely what happened on the 2nd of May 1991, this was an armed conflict but it was Croat policemen that got killed. Right?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from that incident onwards, you say that these Serb families were afraid and that many of them started leaving, if I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were afraid or not. But as soon as the school year was over, a teacher or, rather, two teachers who lived in our street took their children and went to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these people ever come back? Can you remember any such thing?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I never saw them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If people went away for such a long time, what about people who were employed? Did they simply leave their jobs? Can you remember any such cases from the hospital, for instance, where you worked?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: The Borovo Kombinat was working still but was beginning to stop working. I cannot tell you the exact day in September but a colleague who worked with me in sterilisation left but she went to Croatia. The reason for her departure is something that I don't know about and therefore I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was a general one. Was that a trend? Did you notice that? Did you notice that many people no longer came to work? Were there any problems in this respect in hospital? Did the then-director of the hospital have some problems on account of that?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I just told you that a colleague who worked with me left, one of them left earlier, one of them left later, and I cannot confirm anything about others. I can only tell you about the colleagues who worked with me in the sterilisation department and who were in charge of central sterilisation. Instead of them we then had Magda Cerevic and Ilonka Novak. They came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall from that time, that is to say who was the director of your hospital before Dr. Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I think it was Dr. Rade Popovic who was the director, but I'm not 100 per cent sure. I think it was him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you're right. But do you remember that he or the person who was the director before Mrs. Vesna Bosanac, do you remember that he was replaced and that he had problems officially, precisely because he granted leave of absence to many of his employees who did not show up for work? Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I did not hear about that. I only heard about Dr. Stanimirovic who was there before Mrs. Bosanac, and I heard that Dr. Rade Popovic went to Montenegro. That's what I heard. I don't know where he went, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was your own boss at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: You mean of surgery? The surgical department?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Dr. Ivankovic. And afterwards, when the war broke out, Dr. Njavro was in charge of everything and he made a great effort, conducted surgery, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So first it was Dr. Ivankovic and then it was Dr. Njavro; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: That's what I heard. Dr. Ivankovic was the head of our department. When Dr. Sokacic retired, then he became head of the department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dr. Ivankovic stay there throughout the war? Did he carry out operations like all other doctors?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that pertain to other doctors or, rather, surgeons?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Manojlovic was there, Dr. Stanojevic, Dr. Njavro, Dr. Ivankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me how records of patients were kept at the time, books, notebooks? Could you please be so kind as to tell me?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: We had a clerk, Vera Graf, who was in charge of these records, with nurse Biba. Now, how they kept these records, how they wrote things down, I was not there, and I cannot tell you about this. But I know that they were the ones who kept records. For how long, until when, that is again something I cannot tell you about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell me whether you saw what these books or ledgers looked like. How were these books kept? You probably gave information and you probably participated in that.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: These books were kept where the clinic was, the -- of the surgery and that's where the administration offices were. For the most part, I was downstairs where the sterilisation rooms are and where the corridors are and the atomic shelter. Sometimes I would go to the clinic to help out but I was not involved in any other details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the conflict, I assume that there was an increasingly higher number of the wounded brought to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sure there were wounded civilians, but I'm interested in the wounded soldiers. Were any wounded members of the ZNG brought in or Croatian police, JNA or any other formation?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Our hospital admitted all wounded persons regardless of their ethnicity or affiliation. We admitted them and treated them. Later on, when there was no longer room at the hospital, those who were slightly wounded were transferred to Borovo Komerc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you personally in contact or were you able to be in contact with those wounded persons, or because of the nature of your work, you were unable to have contact with them?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Given the nature of my work, I had fewer contacts with these wounded persons than my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to see if there were any such cases, that there were some armed men guarding certain patients or rather wounded persons? I'm specifically referring to the wounded JNA members.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you that because I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "I didn't see that," is that because you had very few contacts with them, in view of your work in the sterilisation department?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I told you how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether the hospital had any security personnel? Were there any security personnel outside or inside?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you that. I wasn't involved in that. I wasn't even interested in that. I worked inside the building and I wouldn't be able to tell you what was happening outside of it. I didn't move out frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the hospital had telephone lines with the outside world, and if these lines were disconnected, do you know when?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I know that the telephone lines were operational, but until what time I wouldn't be able to tell you, because that wasn't part of my work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to enter and spend some time in the room which was the office of your hospital director, Dr. Vesna Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. But there was no need and I wasn't interested. There was no reason for me to enter that room and spend time there. I did my work to the best of my abilities. I did not concern myself with other people's business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you whether you entered that room and if you did, whether you remember what items there were in that room.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we spoke just now about relations, you said that relations deteriorated after the Borovo Selo incident. Immediately prior to that, did they start erecting barricades in certain villages around Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I couldn't say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that you can't say anything about that, is it because you don't remember it? Do you remember people discussing that there were barricades which prevented them from travelling from one place to another?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I remember that people discussed that. Now, as to who manned these barricades and where they were erected, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You described to us how little you moved about. You said that you didn't leave Vukovar at all, that you just moved between your house and the hospital and later on you stayed at the hospital constantly.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that the area where you lived, which was called Sajmiste, was quite close or relatively close to the barracks of the JNA in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. I don't know the distance, but my street is close to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that sometime during that period, before the event on the 25th of August, there were any problems with the barracks, that the barracks was besieged, that water and electricity supply were cut off? Did you hear this discussed at work?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that during that time, and by this I'm also referring to the time before the Borovo Selo incident and after that, there were cases when the houses were blown up, when houses were torched, and that the Borba newsstand was blown up?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: That was discussed. People said that the Borba newsstand and Vjesnik newsstand were blown up, and that all kinds of newsstands were being blown up. I don't know who did it, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that both types of newsstands were blown up, what do you have in mind? You mean that it wasn't just the Borba newsstand but also others?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Vjesnik newsstand. You yourself said Borba newsstand. This is why I said both newsstands, Vjesnik was the Croatian evening newspaper. And then we also had Vecernje Novosti and Borba from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That's precisely why I asked you this because the Trial Chamber may not know it. What about the cases when houses were blown up? It was quite easy to establish who the owner was; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: As I went home from work, I could see that there were already some houses that were destroyed, both in my street and in some other streets. But regardless of whose house it was, whether it was owned by a Serb or by a Croat, when a shell landed or another type of an explosive, houses were destroyed regardless of whom they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that when it comes to the shelling, but that wasn't what I was driving at. My question pertained to the period long before the shelling of Vukovar started. It pertained to the period prior to that, while all of you still lived there together in, let us say, normal circumstances. That was the time when these newsstands were destroyed and the houses and so on. I'm now referring to the houses which were intentionally blown up.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I just told you about newsstands and houses and there is nothing else I can tell you about. I don't know about somebody coming in and destroying houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Madam, do you know who Tomislav Mercep was?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I've heard of him. I didn't know him. I saw him only upon reaching Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what post he held in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Based on the stories, he supposedly took over the Territorial Defence, and organised it. I don't know whether this is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that during that period of time, when he organised the Territorial Defence, it was rumoured that certain people went missing, that they were either killed or simply disappeared? Do you remember this being discussed?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that you can't confirm that, does this mean that you don't remember it, you don't remember hearing something of this nature?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I don't remember hearing anything similar nor did I ever discuss this with anybody at great length. I told you earlier that I was focused on my house, my family, and my work, which was supposed to provide my living in old age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now that you have mentioned your house and you told us who lived in that area, please tell us: Did you get along well with your neighbours, especially Serb neighbours? Did you ever have any problems prior to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement given to the investigators, you said that in addition to what your husband did and that you told us about, he was also a member of the military police. You never mentioned this today. So please tell us when was this?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: When they took him away from the hospital and then when he came back he said that he was going to the military police. Now, as to whether he actually went there or not, I don't know. That he belonged to the military police. I don't know who organised the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you are definitely referring to the military police which existed within the National Guards Corps, the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's clarify this further. You are now referring to the period of time when he went to the Eltz castle?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mrs. Bucko. Thank you for your answers. I have no further questions for you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I've finished my cross examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Domazet. I think I might do the usual thing, Mr. Borovic, and have the break now so that you could start afterwards. We will adjourn now and resume at 20 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Cross-examined by Mr. Borovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, my name is Borivoj Borovic. I'm Defence counsel for Miroslav Radic. Madam, my first question for you: In the neighbourhood where you lived, throughout that period of time, you said that at least half of the houses were owned by the Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the majority of people move out of their houses in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: The teacher did, Milicevic, and then Radicic, Vracaric left. Mrs. Guzic went to her daughter in Belgrade. Her daughter was called Milica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, I wasn't going to ask you to give me all of the names. I just wanted to know whether the majority of them left their houses in that period leading up to November. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I think so. I think they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you talk to any of them before they left their houses?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that your husband was a member of the ZNG, the National Guards Corps, and a member of the 204th Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. They said that that's what it was called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that in almost every street, people were organised and took turns keeping guard. What period of time was it?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: It was in July, but I wouldn't be able to give you the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Do you know who procured weapons for them, the weapons that they had had while they stood guard?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that in almost every street, in various neighbourhoods, there were people standing guard. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. In various neighbourhoods, yes. Sajmiste had their people, Mitnica had their people. The people were organised in various neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And when did you learn that, that in various neighbourhoods this was organised?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: In our street, when they started organising this, when they asked people to join, this is when I learned it. It was either mid- or late July but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You say that they started gathering people, these members of civilian protection. Who did that?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: People from the street went house by house asking for volunteers in order to organise them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know any of the names of the organisers and was your husband among them?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No. My husband was not one of the organisers. He was invited to join, and agreed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were living together, do you know who invited him and when?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say who was the first one who started organising this in our local community. Therefore, I wouldn't want to give any names because I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Madam. When your husband joined this group? Did he join the 204th Brigade or was that only later?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Listen, I wouldn't be able to confirm to you when the National Guards Corps was founded or the 204th Brigade. It was only in Zagreb that I heard that the brigade was called 204th. But I can't tell you the date or the month when it was established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You said that when your husband came to visit you in the hospital, they took him away from there and it was then that you learned from him that he was going to be a member of military police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who took him away, were they uniformed?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No. They wore civilian clothes. This is how they came to the hospital and they took several of our husbands away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember did they have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I don't know. We were in that corridor down there where I've been telling you all the time that the central sterilisation was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see the moment when they were taken away or not?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I did. Because I was having a very hard time because my husband was being taken away but nevertheless he had to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that he did not leave of his own free will or is it the way you said, that they forced him to go?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: When they came to get him and when they picked up a few of them, they left. Nobody asked, do you agree or do you disagree. At least I never heard any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he opposed to leaving? Did he want to stay?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I was opposed to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your husband? I hope that he has a say, too.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Well, he does, but I really cannot tell you how it was then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What are the other husbands who were taken away? Do you remember some of the names?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Stanek, Behlic, my husband, I cannot remember any others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How many of them were there approximately, in terms of numbers, not names?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I don't think that there were that many that time when they were there. I don't think that too many of them were taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. When they took them away, what were your husbands wearing at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: My husband had normal clothes on. I don't know whether he was wearing jeans or regular trousers. I can't say now. And also, he had a vest, a shirt, a jacket like any person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the other husbands who happened to be at the hospital? Did they perhaps have some kind of hospital clothing on?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I didn't see any hospital clothing on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The previous question was: How come they happened to be there precisely on that day when your husband came to visit you? How come these other husbands were in hospital too?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Well, wives probably brought their husbands to hospital there because they worked there and then they brought their families along with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You'll have to try to help us a bit now. Were they employed? How could they simply be brought to a hospital and do nothing? I asked you intentionally so that I would not confuse you. I asked you whether they had any hospital clothing. What were they doing there?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: When my husband came to see me, he was working but wearing civilian clothes. He was closing windows with wooden boards so that we would not feel cold. Our driver, Sime, and he were doing that. I don't know whether there was anybody else because I didn't really follow them trying to see what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These husbands, did they do anything else or did they just hide there in the hospital, if you don't mind my asking?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I don't mind you asking anything. I don't know the answer and I cannot give you an answer. I won't give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When he was taken away and when he became a military policeman, according to what you heard, in the meantime, did your husband come to visit you in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now describe that uniform of his that he wore when he came to see you?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No. Because he wore civilian clothing and he did not wear a uniform then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell us the reason why he came in civilian clothing if he was a military policeman? What was the reason? Safety, security, some other reason?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I don't know. But I think that he did not even have a uniform. I never saw a uniform on him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And in November when he came to see you, you said that he was wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Not true, not true. I never saw my husband in a uniform and he did not come in uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: He came in a dirty jacket and trousers and in an awful looking pair of shoes. And he looked unkempt, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we will have occasion to hear your husband very soon, I think that his information speaks to the contrary, but we'll ask him about it.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Just go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the month of November, when he came for one day, did he know that evacuation would follow or not?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: He said to me that the town had fallen, and that Stanek told them in the morning to go to the hospital, that that was the best, and that that is where he should seek shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Why would it be best for him there? Why should he seek shelter at the hospital? Can you explain this to us??

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what your husband said to you?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: That's what my husband said to me. But why Mr. Sremac said that to him, probably on account of the fact that I worked there and probably because he was taken from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I tell you that he had reason as a member of the ZNG, which is undisputable now even according to what you said, to hide in the hospital so that the JNA would not arrest him, can you confirm that? Is that a valid possibility, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I cannot answer that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. At any point in time, except for that list of 15 or 16 husbands that you spoke about, did you ever ask nurse Kolesar to write your husband's name down on the evacuation list?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Why did you do that, if you knew that he had just come from the ZNG and that there was no place for him on that list?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I don't see how you can keep saying that, that he was with the ZNG, if he did not wear a uniform. And if he was in our neighbourhood, in our house for as long as he could, and in the streets. And then he came to see me at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm claiming that for the simple reason that you yourself said that he was a member of the ZNG. Please let me finish. You yourself said that he became a member of the military police, and when asked by my colleague, Mr. Domazet, you said that it was the military police or the ZNG, and later on in Zagreb you found out that the brigade he belonged to was the 204th Brigade. This is the information that you have provided to us, and that's why I'm asking you whether as a member of the ZNG, he did what he did. That is why I claim that he was a member of the ZNG, on the basis of your very own statements. But let us go on. So it is an assertion based on what you've been saying. But let us proceed. You said that his military position was in the Eltz castle.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Well, that's what was being said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he say to you? What was he doing there? I hope you talked about it.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. He said that there were some works of art there, that they needed to be put away in order to be preserved, and I don't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he tell you later on whether they managed to put them away, to preserve them? What has he been doing or, rather, what did he do then? It's been 15 years. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: As far as I know, all of it stayed in the basement, because no one could take anything out. So they didn't really manage to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If I tell you that the mayor, as you said, of the town of Vukovar at that time, had previously passed a decision to move all these works of art out of Eltz castle before it was taken by the ZNG, can you support this assertion of mine, or do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I just know about the things that I discussed with my husband.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So your husband comes on the 19th, and you mentioned a few persons who came along with him. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about these people? Did they belong to the ZNG, to the best of your knowledge, on that day, or later on?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you ask your husband how come that he came in with these people? Did they come together?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Well, he came together with them because he was taken from the hospital together with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who Mr. Kolak is? Have you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was this man?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Young men from the neighbouring street which used to be called Patkovica. I know them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether they were in the ZNG, the sons of this Mr. Kolak?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Well, look, I cannot say that the -- what it exactly was, the ZNG, they used to call it the National Guards Corps, and then later on the 204th Brigade. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, I'm asking you very carefully. I'm not asking you what the ZNG means, what it stands for, when the 204th Brigade was established. Were the Kolaks the members of a military or paramilitary formation?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: How can I tell you about them?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On that day, when your husband changed your clothes [as interpreted] on the 19th because he was dirty, and you also said that he washed his face. What about his other -- what about these other men who came from Eltz with him? Did they also bathe and change?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Well, they didn't really bathe and change. I know about him. He took off his jacket and washed up. I really can't say about the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On that occasion, when your husband was changing, were these other husbands who had been taken away from hospital present as well?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: We were not together because they were all at different places where their wives worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we conclude, then, that everybody had a workplace by their wives?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Well, not by their wives. I cannot say that he was with me all the time when he was in the hospital. I've already told you that he helped our driver, Sime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have to interrupt you, but that was earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'm asking you about the 19th, when they came to hospital. And you say that they were employed with their wives?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No, I did not say employed. That is what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you tell us, then, what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: On the 19th, my husband came and he was down there, but he was not with me all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know how many of these husbands of yours were there at the Eltz castle? Did your husband ever tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I don't know the exact numbers. I know a few names, and I can give them to you any time of day and night, whenever you want.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since I don't want -- can you tell me how many members of the ZNG were there?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I cannot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, see, you cannot. Thank you. Can you explain why you locked up your husband at a given point in time?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I didn't lock him up. I wanted to lock him up, though, so that he would stay so that I would go to the plaster room together with my colleagues. But he didn't want to. He left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Why did you want to lock him up?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I cannot say now. I don't know the reason. That's what came to my mind that very moment. And why? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you don't know what happened around the hospital. My question is the following: While you were employed there, did the hospital have its own internal security? Did you have any security, any guards?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I did not participate in that, and I don't know whether there was any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And in this period, did you leave the hospital building during those two or three months?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I came from home and I worked in the hospital, and I didn't leave the hospital after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And at any point in time, did you go upstairs from the basement during those two or three months? Did you go to the entrance, to the door?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I only went to the hall of the internal medicine department and, when necessary, I took the container with the sterile material so that the wounded could have their wounds dressed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And in that hall and by that door, did you see armed policemen guarding you?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I did not see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was no one there?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I am telling you that I did not see them, because I walked upstairs and I went straight to the hall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. Thank you. In this period of time, did you notice what Vesna Bosanac was doing and what Dr. Njavro was doing?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: As for Dr. Vesna Bosanac, I cannot say anything because she's on one side of the building and I'm at the other side of the building. As for Dr. Njavro, I can confirm that day and night he went down to see the wounded in the shelter and the halls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Vesna Bosanac come to see the wounded where you were?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I saw her a few times when she came but I cannot give you the exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Before these armed conflicts took place, you know the layout of the hospital very well, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The main entrance to the hospital, are there any steps before you enter the hospital through the main entrance? Are there any steps there?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. Steps that take you to the ground floor as we call it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the main entrance?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And on the other side, or just a moment, please. On the other side of the hospital, are there any steps there too or do you just walk straight to the door?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: There are no steps, and there is a slight slope leading to the emergency entrance for the surgery and all other emergencies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you came in and stopped going out, did you see a red cross flag in the hospital compound or not?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: On the roof there was a marking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What marking, where?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Well, there was this red cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you be more specific? What was marked by a red cross?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Well, up on the roof, the hospital was marked by a red cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've heard you. But could you please explain more specifically, what kind of a sign was this, a marking? Was it drawn or what was it?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: How it got up there, I really don't know. I saw something white and red, but whether this was drawn or how it was placed up there, that I don't know, and I don't know who placed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it placed up there so that it could be seen from an airplane too?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Well, it was on the roof.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But how could you see it if you were not viewing it from way up?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: It's a slanted roof and on that side I saw it. Whether there were any other things elsewhere, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you see it? What period of time was it?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: In the beginning, I really wouldn't be able to tell you more specifically. I don't remember what month it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who placed it?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't want to put to you what other witnesses stated here; no reason for that. Did you ever hear of a JNA soldier called Sasa Jovic?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: The one that was wounded?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. I think there was a Zoran and then a Sasa, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Since you heard about them, what did you hear about Sasa, when did you hear it, when was he brought to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I heard from my colleagues that he had been wounded. Where and how, I don't know. I heard that he was at the hospital. I personally didn't see him. I didn't take care of him. And I know nothing about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Why did your colleague then tell you and how come you remembered this so that you could reply right away when I mentioned his name, Sasa Jovic?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I suppose that he was Sasa Jovic, but since my son is called Zoran, I remember that another one, another wounded person, was also called Zoran.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how come do you then remember Sasa Jovic? Was it by his first name or his last name?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I didn't remember either his first or his last name. It's just that you mentioned him, so I thought you were right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it mean that they were the exceptions, these two JNA soldiers, who were there in the hospital wounded and that this is how you remembered them, because all the rest were members of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how did you then remember them?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I didn't pay any attention to the people's origin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you have any members of the ZNG hospitalised in your hospital?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Everybody who was wounded was brought to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was about the ZNG members.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I can't answer that because I didn't keep the records. I don't know who was what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know somebody from your street, do you know their first names and surnames, people who belonged to the civilian protection? And did any of them come to the hospital seeking help?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We concluded based on your testimony that your husband was active in the military sense. Do you know whether Dr. Vesna Bosanac's husband was also active in the military?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the husband of Dr. Striber?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who nurse Marica is? She used to work in the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Listen, it's a quite common first name. I don't know who you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person with the first name of Marica? Do you know any last names? Was there any such nurse?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: We had several women with that first name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Give us an example.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Well, we had Marica Stanek. People also referred to me as Marica, even though my name is Mara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the same Stanek who came with your husband?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the nurse whose surname is Bradaric?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: There was that last name, a person with that last name, but I can't remember what she looked like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that her husband was a member of police force?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us in that three-month period of time, how many doctors there were at the Vukovar Hospital, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I can't say that. I would now have to enumerate them, all of those whom I can remember, in order to be able to give you a number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I told you that there were 36 of them, 36 physicians at the Vukovar Hospital, can you confirm or deny that?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you deny that there were that many?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I can't deny that either. I don't know the number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. If I tell you that there was 107 medical technicians, nurses and others at the Vukovar Hospital, would you be able to confirm that number? These are your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I can give you the same reply. I didn't keep the records, I didn't show any interest in that, and I don't know the figures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We mentioned some of your colleagues and their husbands. If you're interested in the information I was able to acquire so far in this trial, you will see that I learned that the husbands of almost all of the nurses were militarily engaged. What would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I cannot comment what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you understand -- do you speak English?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you gave your statement to the investigators in 1995, did they read the statement out to you before you signed it or, rather, did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I think I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you signed it, was this statement read out to you?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Quickly, speedily, yes. It was read out to me. I perhaps didn't even think it through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But nevertheless you signed it?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Well, I was beside myself, just like I am today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm trying to be as fair as possible. I don't think I have been unfair so far.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Based on you, I would have to confirm all kinds of things, even the ones I know nothing about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. When you gave your statement, did you draw a sketch of the hospital or parts of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could I have the assistance of the usher, please? I want this sketch to be placed on the ELMO. The Prosecution already has this sketch, so I didn't provide them with a copy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll wait just a little bit. Would you be so kind and lift up the sketch? I'm talking now to the technicians. Just a little bit more. Do you see the signature?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please don't interrupt. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I was just about to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just tell me. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can we now lower it a little bit, the sketch? Can you -- yes. Thank you. Did you draw the sketch?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who drew it for you?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know? You never saw it? You just signed it.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I didn't see the sketch then. And you, if you want, you can pass it on to somebody who will analyse the handwriting and see whether it's mine or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When you gave the statement you gave it voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the sketch, if I'm not mistaken, was not something that you discussed?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you never saw it until today?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I saw it --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: When I arrived in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that this was not your sketch, that you didn't draw it.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I said that and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in order to be as efficient as possible, to contribute to the economy of the proceedings, I will now conclude with my cross-examination. No, just a second. I apologise. Before I conclude completely, I would like to tender this sketch into evidence because, after all, there is a signature and the witness just confirmed that it was hers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 128.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have already thanked you, Your Honour, I will now formally conclude my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody. Cross-examined by Mr. Bulatovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Bucko, I am attorney Bulatovic. I am one of the lawyers for Sljivancanin. I will now be putting questions to you. Please give us your answers slowly. Since my colleagues and the Prosecutor spent quite a long time examining you, I will try to conclude before the end of business today. My first question to you: In addition to the statement that you gave to the OTP investigators, did you ever, between 1991 and today give any other statement to anybody else, any written or any other kind of statement about these events?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. So your husband came on the 19th in the morning, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to his arrival to the hospital, were there any other husbands of your colleagues there, and if so, do you know when they arrived?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: There were husbands there, and as to when they arrived, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what they did, these husbands of your colleagues? What they did during their stay in the hospital? What kinds of jobs? I know that you discussed this somewhat but it remained --

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Unclear. And I'm unable to clear this entirely for you because I told you I did not concern myself with that. I don't know what they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you sent your daughter to Miklosevci. You said that your daughter-in-law went to Krk and that after sometime your son joined her. Can you tell me when this was, approximately? Do you know at least the month?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Approximately my daughter left in late August or perhaps early September. I don't know for sure. My father-in-law lived in that village and she went there. I thought that perhaps I would be able to visit her when I was free. However, I wasn't able to do that. When she left the village, based on what she told us they went to Ilok, and then from Ilok the army took her away and somehow she arrived in Djakovo to stay with my family there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was just interested in the time frame, not in the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: My son left as did my daughter-in-law. My granddaughter was born on the 18th of August. My son left in late August, or perhaps early September, to join his wife and daughter. And he didn't come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether any other neighbours of yours, colleagues, friends, acquaintances, sent members of their families outside of Vukovar during this period of time? Just tell me yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I know about some.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, do you know whether sometime during August 1991, the media, and by this I mean television or radio, did they broadcast the information that there was -- that there was going to be an evacuation?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. On the 19th, you said that you went to the hall looking for your husband and that there were a lot of people there. Is this the hall that one enters after going through the main entrance?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: This is the hall right next to the main entrance of the hospital, taking the steps up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many steps?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I don't know. I went there numerous times but I never counted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: More than five or less?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: More than five.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. When you enter the hall, are there corridors going to the left or the right or straight?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: This is the hall that takes you either to the right or to the left. It takes you to the internal diseases ward and then there are steps leading to the ground floor and then stairs leading upstairs. There was also an elevator there, freight elevator, and the one for us personnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In your view, how many civilians there were in that area in the hall and corridors?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you that. I was just looking for my husband. If somebody asked me for my name, perhaps I would not have been able to answer. I was that excited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let us turn to the meeting that you described on the 19th of November 1991. You said that you weren't sure what time it was. When you gave your statement to the Prosecutor, you said that a JNA officer approached you. This is what is stated in your statement. And then he said that all nurses had to come to the plaster room?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes. We were told to come to the meeting in the plaster room on the 19th. As to the time of the day, whether it was -- it was in the afternoon, but I don't know what time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All I'm interested in is whether you were told this by a JNA officer, as your statement reads.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I can't tell ranks. I don't know. The man wore a uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that once you got there, there was another officer standing there whom you identified as my client, Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I didn't know that he was Veselin Sljivancanin. He introduced himself to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell the Court and tell us in greater detail what you remember about that conversation conducted on the 19th in the afternoon with the medical staff?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: As far as I remember, that's as far as I can tell you. In the plaster room, the gentleman introduced himself to us. I can't tell you whether he said he was a captain or a major. He said to us, "I am Veselin Sljivancanin. Dr. Bosanac is no longer anything. You will have a new director. I don't know his rank. I don't know his name. You medical staff may remain working here. There is no need for you to be afraid. The hospital will continue operating. You will work here." And I don't know what else to tell you. I have already described this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. Thank you. In that meeting, do you remember whether there were any doctors?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I'm not 100 per cent sure that Dr. Matos was inside. As for the others, I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember how long this meeting went on?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I don't know. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether at that meeting Mr. Sljivancanin made a proposal? Maybe you already said this but never mind -- that you take a few days of leave and then return to work?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On the evening of the 19th, you're there in that room with your husband and some other colleagues. Since you were talking about everything, were you commenting upon what happened in the plaster room and also these changes, changing the director of the hospital, the offer to take a few days of leave and work again? Did you talk about it?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: We talked about it a little bit, because I personally felt that some fear was instilled in me, but how, I really cannot say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 20th, in the morning, there was a meeting in the plaster room again?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember who called you and informed you about the meeting in the plaster room on the 20th in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: A younger man in uniform knocked at the door in the morning and told us to go to the plaster room. Then I told my other colleagues, let's go. And he went further on asking other people to come, walking down the corridor, down to the atomic shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that at the moment when you arrived in the plaster room there were already medical staff members in the plaster room and after you arrived there others came after you did?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any doctors in the plaster room then?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not a single one?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. I do not recall seeing any one of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This meeting on the 20th, in the morning, in the plaster room, do you remember how long it went on?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that either because I do not remember how long it lasted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the content of the meeting, the things people said?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Like on the previous day, that day we were also told that we should stay on working, that we should take a few days of leave and stay with our families for a few days and that the hospital would go on working and that we would have this new director.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that during the course of the meeting itself, a colleague informed you that your husband had arrived and you talked about this. So you left?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you talk to your husband?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the meeting still on in the plaster room during that time?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Because I came back to the plaster room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how long you stayed after having returned from seeing your husband? So how long did this last?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly. Well, you can reach your own conclusion. While I was talking to Mr. Sljivancanin, I was making this list, he was in the plaster all the time -- room all the time. He said that he would bring our husbands. Now, how long this went on, I don't know. Who sent -- who he sent to bring these husbands, I don't know. I don't know who went to fetch our husbands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. All these conversations that you're referring to now and these meetings with Mr. Sljivancanin that have to do with lists and handing over lists, are all of them taking place within the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MARA BUCKO
utterances.text: Part of them took place within the hospital and then I wanted to open the door and to give this further on in the corridor but I was not given that opportunity. There were other staff members of ours in the corridor and there were their husbands. I wanted them to be included in the list too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, on the basis of what did you write down 17 names? Is that your own recollection, that these people were there, or did you have any other information as to who you should put on that list? You said 15 or 16 names.
